record.paper_title: The origin and evolution of transition discs: successes, problems and open questions
record.original_question: If planets are responsible for mm-bright transition discs, how is the planetary-mobility problem avoided—either by preventing the gap-opening planet from migrating inward into the small-hole regime or by causing the transition-disc spectral signature to disappear before the system would overproduce accreting, high-mm-flux, small-hole discs that are not observed?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a model of a gaseous protoplanetary disc around a young star in which a giant planet, embedded in the disc, opens an annular gap by exerting tidal torques on the surrounding gas. The disc is termed a "transition disc" if it exhibits a characteristic spectral energy distribution showing a deficit of near- and mid-infrared emission (indicating an inner cavity or hole) together with strong (sub-)millimetre continuum emission from cold outer dust. Define the "hole size" as the radius of the inner cavity carved by the planet, and call a transition disc "mm-bright" if its millimetre continuum flux exceeds a fixed threshold typical of the brightest observed sources. Within standard viscous disc theory coupled with Type I/II planetary migration, a gap-opening planet generally migrates inward on a timescale comparable to or shorter than the disc lifetime, while continuing to accrete gas through the gap. Empirically, mm-bright transition discs with small hole sizes (e.g. cavity radius less than about 10 AU) and simultaneously high accretion rates are essentially absent from observed samples, whereas mm-bright transition discs with large holes are common.

Construct a self-consistent disc–planet evolution model (specifying the surface-density evolution, viscous α, planet migration prescription, gas accretion across the gap, and dust dynamics determining mm flux) such that:

(a) a giant planet capable of producing an mm-bright transition disc with a large hole does not subsequently migrate inward into the regime of small holes while the disc remains mm-bright and accreting; or

(b) the observational transition-disc signature (infrared deficit together with high mm flux) reliably disappears before the planet–disc system would otherwise populate the empirically forbidden region of high mm flux, small hole, and ongoing accretion.

Determine quantitative conditions on the disc and planet parameters under which (a) or (b) holds, and demonstrate that the resulting predicted population of transition discs is consistent with the observed scarcity of accreting, mm-bright, small-hole systems.
artifact.status_search_result: The "planetary-mobility problem" identified by Clarke & Owen (2013) for transition discs remains an open challenge in the protoplanetary-disc community. Subsequent literature on transition-disc populations and planet–disc interaction (e.g. Owen 2016 review; Owen & Kollmeier 2019; van der Marel reviews 2022–2023) continues to flag the absence of accreting, mm-bright, small-hole discs as unexplained, with no consensus mechanism shown to robustly avoid the forbidden region in parameter space.

status_evidence.claim: The problem is identified as an outstanding question in the transition-disc literature.

status_evidence.title: van der Marel review of transition discs
status_evidence.snippet: The origin of transition discs and the role of embedded planets remain debated, with population-level tensions between observed mm fluxes, hole sizes, and accretion rates not yet resolved.
status_evidence.claim: Recent reviews continue to treat the population mismatch as unresolved.
